Expectation1: Maintain regular communication with family members
Situation1: The grandparent learns that a family member is dealing with a significant personal crisis.
Expectation2: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation2: Your friend calls, sounding very upset, and asks if you have a moment to talk about a recent argument with their partner.
Story: My phone buzzed twice in quick succession. First, a message from my daughter: “Grandpa, can you call? Mom’s not doing well.” I knew from our regular chats that things had been tough lately, but this sounded urgent. My heart clenched with worry—my family counted on me to be present, to check in, to hold us together when things got rough. I was already reaching for the phone when it rang again. This time, it was my old friend, Tom. His voice trembled, “Can you talk? I just had a huge fight with Lisa. I don’t know what to do.” Tom had always been there for me, and I knew how much he needed someone to listen right now. I stared at the phone, torn. My family needed me, but so did my friend. Both expected my support, my time, my ear. I felt the weight of their needs pressing in from both sides, my chest tight with the fear of letting someone down.
